questions.stem: A value increases from 5 to 20. By what factor did it increase?
questions.explanation: Factor = new ÷ original = 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

questions.stem: A value decreases from 18 to 6. By what factor did it decrease?
questions.explanation: 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so it decreased by a factor of 3.

questions.stem: At constant propagation speed, what happens to sound travel distance if travel time triples?
questions.explanation: d = ct; with c constant, distance is directly proportional to time.

questions.stem: In a directly proportional relationship y = kx, what happens to y when x is halved?
questions.explanation: In y = kx, halving x halves y.

questions.stem: In the same medium, frequency increases from 3 MHz to 6 MHz. What happens to wavelength?
questions.explanation: With c constant, c = fλ, so doubling f halves λ.

questions.stem: In the same medium, frequency decreases to one-quarter of its original value. What happens to wavelength?
questions.explanation: Quartering f makes λ four times longer.

questions.stem: What is the period of a 5 MHz ultrasound wave?
A wave has a period of 0.5 µs. What is its frequency?
Which pair of quantities is reciprocal?
questions.explanation: Frequency and period satisfy f = 1/T.

questions.stem: Frequency decreases from 4 MHz to 2 MHz. What happens to the period?
questions.explanation: Halving the frequency doubles the reciprocal period.

questions.stem: Two variables are inversely proportional. If the first is halved, the second:
questions.explanation: Inverse: halving one variable doubles the other.

questions.stem: Two variables are inversely proportional. If the first is multiplied by 5, the second:
questions.explanation: Inverse: multiplying one by 5 multiplies the other by 1/5.

questions.stem: Echo return time is directly proportional to reflector depth. A reflector moves from 2 cm to 8 cm. By what factor does return time change?
questions.explanation: Depth changes by 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so return time changes by the same factor.

questions.stem: A reflector moves from 12 cm to 4 cm. What happens to the echo return time?
options: It increases by a factor of 3
questions.explanation: Depth falls to one-third, so return time falls to one-third.

questions.stem: The inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength (c = fλ) holds when:
options: Sound travels in the same medium
questions.explanation: c = fλ gives an inverse relationship only for constant speed (same medium).

questions.stem: Power and intensity are directly proportional only when:
questions.explanation: I = P/A; intensity tracks power directly only when area is constant.

questions.stem: Given c = d/t, which equation solves for time?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides of c = d/t appropriately: t = d/c.

questions.stem: Given c = fλ, which equation solves for wavelength?
questions.explanation: Divide both sides of c = fλ by f: λ = c/f.

questions.stem: Given f = 1/T, which equation solves for period?
questions.explanation: Invert f = 1/T: T = 1/f.

questions.stem: Given I = P/A, which equation solves for beam area?
questions.explanation: Multiply by A, divide by I: A = P/I.

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for propagation speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance per time (m/s).

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz.

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for period?
questions.explanation: Period is a time, in seconds.

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for intensity?
questions.explanation: Intensity is power per unit area (W/cm²).

questions.stem: In d = ct, with c in m/s and t in s, the result d has units of:
questions.explanation: (m/s) × s = m.

questions.stem: If power is in mW and area is in cm², intensity from I = P/A is expressed in:
questions.explanation: mW ÷ cm² = mW/cm².

questions.stem: What is the wavelength of 2 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue (c = 1540 m/s)?
An echo comes from a reflector 4 cm deep (c = 1540 m/s). What is the round-trip time?
Which prefix represents 10³?
questions.explanation: Kilo = 10³.

questions.explanation: Nano = 10⁻⁹.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(100)?
questions.explanation: 10 to the power 2 is 100.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(1,000,000)?
What is log₁₀(0.001)?
What is log₁₀(1)?
Which exponential statement is equivalent to log₁₀(10,000) = 4?
questions.explanation: A log asks "10 to what power?": 10⁴ = 10,000.

questions.stem: Decibels are used in ultrasound to express:
questions.explanation: Decibels use logarithms to express ratios of intensity or power.

questions.stem: An increase of 10 dB corresponds to an intensity change by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Each 10 dB step is a factor of 10 in intensity.

questions.stem: An increase of 20 dB corresponds to an intensity change by a factor of:
questions.explanation: 20 dB is two 10 dB steps: 10 × 10 = 100.

questions.stem: A negative decibel value indicates:
questions.explanation: Negative dB means attenuation (loss).

questions.stem: A positive decibel value indicates:
questions.explanation: Positive dB means amplification (gain).

questions.stem: On a logarithmic scale, each increment:
questions.explanation: Logarithmic increments multiply by the base.

questions.stem: Why are decibels useful in ultrasound?
options: They avoid the use of ratios
They express very large ranges with manageable numbers
questions.explanation: Logarithms compress huge ranges into manageable numbers.

questions.stem: A 60 dB difference corresponds to an intensity ratio of:
questions.explanation: 60 dB = six 10 dB steps = 10⁶.

questions.stem: A change of −30 dB means intensity becomes:
questions.explanation: −30 dB = three steps of ÷10 = one-thousandth.

questions.stem: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. If amplitude doubles, intensity:
questions.explanation: I ∝ amplitude², so 2² = 4.

questions.stem: If amplitude increases by a factor of 4, intensity increases by a factor of:
If amplitude is cut in half, intensity is multiplied by:
Intensity increases by a factor of 25. By what factor did amplitude change?
Which relationship is linear?
options: Distance and time at constant speed
questions.explanation: d = ct is linear; the others are nonlinear.

questions.stem: A directly proportional relationship is graphed as:
options: A straight line through the origin
A downward-sloping curve that levels off
questions.explanation: y = kx passes through the origin.

questions.stem: An inversely proportional relationship is graphed as:
options: A straight line through the origin
A curve that falls as x increases
questions.explanation: An inverse relationship is a curve that falls as x increases.

questions.stem: A horizontal line on a graph of y versus x shows that:
options: y is directly proportional to x
y is inversely proportional to x
y is proportional to x squared
y remains constant as x changes
questions.explanation: A horizontal line means y does not change with x.

questions.stem: A graph of intensity versus amplitude appears as:
options: An upward curve that becomes progressively steeper
A straight line through the origin
questions.explanation: A squared relationship curves upward and steepens.

questions.stem: On a graph of distance versus time, the slope represents:
questions.explanation: Slope = distance ÷ time = speed.

questions.stem: The side of a square is doubled. Its area:
questions.explanation: Area scales with side squared: 2² = 4.

questions.stem: Power is constant and the beam area increases fourfold. Intensity:
questions.explanation: I = P/A; area ×4 makes intensity ÷4.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, sine is defined as:
questions.explanation: SOH: sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, cosine is defined as:
questions.explanation: CAH: cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.

questions.stem: In a right triangle, tangent is defined as:
questions.explanation: TOA: tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent.

questions.stem: In the memory aid SOH CAH TOA, "TOA" stands for:
questions.explanation: TOA = Tangent, Opposite, Adjacent.

questions.stem: The angle of incidence is measured relative to:
questions.explanation: Angles are measured from the normal, not the interface.

questions.stem: The normal line is:
questions.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the interface.

questions.stem: A beam strikes an interface at 20° from the normal. What is the angle between the beam and the interface?
A beam travels along the normal (perpendicular to the interface). What is its angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: Along the normal, the angle of incidence is 0°.

questions.stem: The angle of incidence is 40°. If the reflection is specular, the angle of reflection is:
questions.explanation: Angle of reflection equals angle of incidence.

questions.stem: What is the value of cos 0°?
A rectangle measures 5 cm by 2 cm. What is its area?
questions.explanation: Area = 5 × 2 = 10 cm².

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is three-dimensional (cm³).

questions.stem: A calculated volume is 150 cm³. What is it in millilitres?
questions.explanation: 1 cm³ = 1 mL.

questions.stem: A box measures 3 cm × 4 cm × 5 cm. What is its volume?
A square has an area of 9 cm². What is the length of one side?
A fluid volume is 2 litres. How many millilitres is this?
Sensitivity is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN).

questions.stem: Specificity is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP).

questions.stem: A test finds 45 true positives and misses 5 patients who have the condition. What is the sensitivity?
A test gives 70 true negatives and 30 false positives. What is the specificity?
Positive predictive value (PPV) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: PPV = TP ÷ (TP + FP).

questions.stem: Negative predictive value (NPV) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: NPV = TN ÷ (TN + FN).

questions.stem: A test produces 60 true positives and 20 false positives. What is the PPV?
A test produces 90 true negatives and 10 false negatives. What is the NPV?
The denominator in the calculation of specificity is:
options: All patients with a positive test
All patients with a negative test
All patients who truly have the condition
All patients who truly do not have the condition
questions.explanation: Specificity uses everyone who truly does not have the condition.

questions.stem: A test with high sensitivity is good at:
options: Detecting most patients who truly have the condition
Excluding most patients who do not have the condition
Predicting disease from a positive result only
questions.explanation: High sensitivity means most true cases are detected.

questions.stem: A false negative is a patient who:
options: Has no condition and tests positive
Has the condition and tests positive
Has the condition and tests negative
Has no condition and tests negative
questions.explanation: A false negative has the condition but tests negative.

questions.stem: Of 200 patients, 50 truly have a condition and the test detects 40 of them. What is the sensitivity?
Which term means to increase by a factor of 2?
questions.explanation: Double means increase by a factor of 2 (multiply by 2).

questions.stem: "Quarters" means a value is:
questions.explanation: Quarters means decrease by a factor of 4 (divide by 4).

questions.stem: "Quadruples" means a value:
questions.explanation: Quadruples means increase by a factor of 4 (multiply by 4).

questions.stem: The reciprocal of a number is:
questions.explanation: A reciprocal is the inverted value: 1 divided by the number.

questions.stem: In mathematical language, the word "factor" implies:
questions.explanation: "Factor" implies multiplication or division, not addition or subtraction.

questions.stem: "Half" describes a value that has:
questions.explanation: Half means decrease by a factor of 2 (divide by 2).

questions.stem: What is the reciprocal of 4?
If frequency triples, the period:
questions.explanation: Frequency and period are reciprocals (T = 1/f), so tripling f makes T one-third.

questions.stem: A linear relationship produces which type of graph?
questions.explanation: Linear relationships change at a constant rate and give a straight-line graph.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a nonlinear relationship from the lecture?
options: Distance increasing with travel time at constant speed
Frequency and period as reciprocals of a straight-line plot
questions.explanation: Intensity varies with amplitude squared, so the rate of change is not constant and the graph is curved.

questions.stem: In a linear relationship, the rate of change is:
questions.explanation: A constant rate of change defines a linear relationship.

questions.stem: The graph of a directly proportional relationship is:
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality gives a straight line passing through the origin (zero).

questions.stem: In direct proportionality, doubling one variable:
questions.explanation: Variables change in the same direction by the same factor; doubling one doubles the other.

questions.stem: Imaging depth and echo return time are:
questions.explanation: Doubling depth doubles the round-trip travel time, so they are directly proportional.

questions.stem: In inverse proportionality, the product of the two variables:
questions.explanation: For inverse proportionality, x × y stays constant.

questions.stem: The graph of an inverse relationship forms:
questions.explanation: Inverse relationships plot as a downward curve.

questions.stem: In an inverse relationship, doubling one variable:
questions.explanation: Variables change in opposite directions; doubling one halves the other.

questions.stem: In a reciprocal relationship, the two variables multiply to equal:
questions.explanation: Reciprocals multiply to equal 1 (e.g., f × T = 1).

questions.stem: Which pair is an example of a reciprocal relationship?
questions.explanation: Frequency and period (and PRF and PRP) are the lecture's examples of reciprocal pairs.

questions.stem: PRF and PRP are:
questions.explanation: PRF = 1/PRP, and PRP = 1/PRF.

questions.stem: Y is directly proportional to z and inversely proportional to k. Which expression fits?
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality to z puts z in the numerator; inverse proportionality to k puts k in the denominator.

questions.stem: If x is directly proportional to y and y increases by a factor of 36, x will:
questions.explanation: Direct proportionality: both variables change by the same factor, so x also increases 36-fold.

questions.stem: If x and y are inversely proportional and x decreases by a factor of 19, y will:
questions.explanation: Inverse proportionality: if x falls by a factor of 19, y rises by a factor of 19.

questions.stem: A is inversely proportional to B. If B is doubled, A:
questions.explanation: Doubling B halves A when they are inversely proportional.

questions.stem: Which is NOT recommended when building a formula sheet?
options: Identifying direct, inverse and reciprocal relationships
Memorizing formulas without understanding the variables
questions.explanation: A good formula sheet records the meaning of each variable and shows how to rearrange it. Memorizing without understanding defeats the purpose.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, a unit:
options: Changes the value of a number
questions.explanation: A unit gives meaning to a number ("10" means nothing until you say 10 km, 10 miles, etc.).

questions.stem: The metric system is based on powers of:
questions.explanation: The metric system is built on powers of 10.

questions.stem: A metric prefix is:
options: A modifier placed before a unit indicating a power of 10
A suffix added after a unit
questions.explanation: A prefix is a modifier placed before a unit to indicate a specific multiplier or power of 10.

questions.stem: The prefix "kilo" represents:
The prefix "milli" represents:
questions.explanation: Milli = 10⁻³ (one-thousandth).

questions.stem: The prefix "micro" represents:
questions.explanation: Micro = 10⁻⁶ (one-millionth).

questions.stem: The prefix "mega" represents:
questions.explanation: Mega = 10⁶ (one million).

questions.stem: The prefix "nano" represents:
questions.explanation: Nano = 10⁻⁹.

questions.stem: The prefix "centi" represents:
questions.explanation: Centi = 10⁻² (one-hundredth).

questions.stem: Convert 4.5 cm to millimetres.
Convert 2 MHz to Hz.
questions.explanation: Mega = 10⁶, so 2 MHz = 2,000,000 Hz.

questions.stem: Convert 15 mm to cm.
Convert 5 ms to seconds.
questions.explanation: Milli = 10⁻³, so 5 ms = 0.005 s.

questions.stem: 13 µs expressed in seconds in scientific notation is:
0.00032 in scientific notation is:
questions.explanation: Move the decimal four places right: 3.2 × 10⁻⁴.

questions.stem: 6,500,000 in scientific notation is:
questions.explanation: Move the decimal six places left: 6.5 × 10⁶.

questions.stem: Length measures:
questions.explanation: Length is a one-dimensional measurement, reported in mm or cm.

questions.stem: Area of a rectangle equals:
questions.explanation: Area (two dimensions) = length × width.

questions.stem: Which is a correct unit of area?
questions.explanation: Area is reported in square units such as cm² or m². cm³ is volume.

questions.stem: Volume is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Volume uses three dimensions: length × width × height.

questions.stem: 1 cm³ is equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 cm³ = 1 mL.

questions.stem: A rectangle is 4 cm long and 3 cm wide. Its area is:
A structure measures 2 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. Its volume in mL is:
questions.explanation: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 cm³, and 1 cm³ = 1 mL, so 30 mL.

questions.stem: Which set lists units of time?
questions.explanation: Time is reported in seconds, milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds.

questions.stem: Which time unit is the smallest?
questions.explanation: Nanosecond (10⁻⁹ s) is smaller than a microsecond (10⁻⁶ s) or millisecond (10⁻³ s).

questions.stem: 1 millisecond equals:
questions.explanation: Milli = 10⁻³, so 1 ms = 0.001 s.

questions.stem: 1000 µs equals:
Which ultrasound application uses logarithms?
questions.explanation: Decibels use logarithms to express large ratios.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(100)?
What is log₁₀(1000)?
questions.explanation: 10³ = 1000, so the logarithm is 3.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(1)?
questions.explanation: 10⁰ = 1, so log₁₀(1) = 0.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(10)?
log₁₀(1000) = 3 written in exponential form is:
questions.explanation: A logarithm is the exponent: log₁₀(1000) = 3 means 10³ = 1000.

questions.stem: Logarithms are useful in ultrasound because they:
questions.explanation: Logs compress large ratios into manageable numbers, which is why decibels use them.

questions.stem: What is log₁₀(0.1)?
sin 30° equals:
questions.explanation: From the trig table, sin 30° = 0.5.

questions.explanation: At 45°, sine and cosine are equal at about 0.707.

cos 30° is approximately:
sin 0° equals:
As an angle increases from 0° to 90°, its cosine:
questions.explanation: Cosine falls from 1 at 0° to 0 at 90°.

questions.stem: Angle conventions require:
questions.explanation: Angles must be measured from a clearly identified reference line.

questions.stem: In reflection and refraction, incidence angles are conventionally measured relative to the:
questions.explanation: Reflection and refraction angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the boundary.

questions.stem: Diagnostic test statistics help determine the:
options: Accuracy and reliability of sonography findings
questions.explanation: Diagnostic test statistics help determine the accuracy and reliability of sonography findings.

questions.stem: Interpreting an anatomic image for a structural abnormality is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Interpreting an anatomic image is a qualitative assessment.

questions.stem: Doppler values and other numeric data are examples of:
questions.explanation: Doppler values and other numeric data are quantitative.

questions.stem: An echocardiogram used to evaluate aortic stenosis is an example of a:
questions.explanation: An echocardiogram evaluating for aortic stenosis is a diagnostic test.

questions.stem: Sensitivity is the ability of a test to correctly identify:
options: Patients who do not have the disease
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the true-positive rate: how well the test detects people who have the condition.

questions.stem: Specificity is the ability of a test to correctly identify:
questions.explanation: Specificity is the true-negative rate: how well the test identifies people without the condition.

questions.stem: Which formula gives sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN).

questions.stem: Which formula gives specificity?
questions.explanation: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP).

questions.stem: Which formula gives positive predictive value (PPV)?
questions.explanation: PPV = TP / (TP + FP): the proportion of positive results that are truly positive.

questions.stem: Which formula gives negative predictive value (NPV)?
questions.explanation: NPV = TN / (TN + FN): the proportion of negative results that are truly negative.

questions.stem: Accuracy is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Accuracy = all correct results divided by all results.

questions.stem: A test finds 90 true positives and misses 10 diseased patients (false negatives). Sensitivity is:
A test has 80 true negatives and 20 false positives. Specificity is:
A test has 45 true positives and 5 false positives. PPV is:
A test has 95 true negatives and 5 false negatives. NPV is:
A study has TP = 40, TN = 50, FP = 5, FN = 5. Accuracy is:
A false negative is a:
options: Diseased patient with a negative test
Healthy patient with a positive test
Healthy patient with a negative test
Diseased patient with a positive test
questions.explanation: A false negative is a patient who has the disease but tests negative.

questions.stem: A false positive is a:
options: Diseased patient with a positive test
Healthy patient with a positive test
Diseased patient with a negative test
Healthy patient with a negative test
questions.explanation: A false positive is a healthy patient who tests positive.

questions.stem: A highly sensitive test is most useful for:
options: Ruling out disease when the result is negative
Ruling in disease when the result is positive
questions.explanation: A highly sensitive test rarely misses disease, so a negative result helps rule disease out.

questions.stem: Pulse timing in Physics 1 involves which parameters?
questions.explanation: Pulse timing covers PRF, PRP and pulse duration.

questions.stem: Attenuation in later modules uses which mathematical tools?
questions.explanation: Attenuation uses ratios, logarithms and decibels.

questions.stem: Which ultrasound task is listed as using mathematics?
questions.explanation: Depth calculations, pulse timing and Doppler velocity estimation all rely on mathematics.

questions.stem: If f = 5 MHz, the period T is:
If the period is 0.5 µs, the frequency is:
If PRP = 200 µs, the PRF is:
questions.explanation: PRF = 1/PRP = 1 / 200 µs = 5000 Hz = 5 kHz.

questions.stem: If imaging depth doubles, round-trip echo time:
questions.explanation: Depth and round-trip time are directly proportional, so doubling depth doubles time.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Relationships may be linear, nonlinear, direct or inverse
All relationships in ultrasound are linear
questions.explanation: Relationships can be linear, nonlinear, direct or inverse, and equations can be rearranged. Logarithms underpin decibels.

questions.stem: Metric prefixes and scientific notation are used mainly to:
options: Simplify very large and very small values
questions.explanation: Prefixes and scientific notation make very large and very small values easier to write and compare.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reciprocal pair of the form a × b = 1?
questions.explanation: 4 × 0.25 = 1, so they are reciprocals.
